tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (bench/bench.cpp, plotted by bench/bars.py). The README names GCC and the flags -std=c++11 -O2 -m64 -march=native, and the README chart's x-axis names the CPU ("Cycles per element (i5-4670k @ 3.4GHz)"), so code, compiler, flags and CPU are all stated; upgraded from C. The GCC version is not stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Approximate, read from the README bar chart (sorting 10^6 ints, cycles per element, i5-4670k @ 3.4GHz) (derived from page data). Vs GCC std::sort, pdqsort is faster on all 8 distributions: shuffled ~113 vs ~220 (~1.9x), shuffled 16 values ~20 vs ~84 (~4x), descending ~7 vs ~34 (~5x), pipe organ ~118 vs ~266 (~2.2x), push front ~45 vs ~319 (~7x), and more than 10x on all equal, ascending and push middle (~3-4 vs ~38-179). Vs std::stable_sort it is faster on shuffled (~113 vs ~273, ~2.4x) and most patterns, but slower on pipe organ (~118 vs ~51) and about equal on push front (~45 vs ~45).
corrections.workload: Median cycles per element (rdtsc, bench/bench.cpp) sorting a std::vector<int> of 10^6 elements under 8 distributions (shuffled, shuffled 16 values, all equal, ascending, descending, pipe organ, push front, push middle), compared to GCC libstdc++ std::sort and std::stable_sort.
corrections.hardware: i5-4670k @ 3.4GHz (stated in the x-axis label of the README benchmark chart)
corrections.caveats: Numbers appear only in a bar-chart image (i.imgur.com/1RnIGBO.png), so the values are approximate readings. The CPU is printed in the chart's axis label (bars.py writes its cpu argument into the xlabel). Not faster than std::stable_sort on pipe organ (~2.3x slower) and about equal on push front. Only 10^6 ints are charted. GCC version and run date are unstated, so the libstdc++ tested is old. No commits since 2021-03-14 (more than 3 years), so abandoned.

notes: Tier upgraded C->A: the CPU the record called unstated is printed on the README chart axis. claimed_speedup overstated the win over std::stable_sort (slower on pipe organ, tie on push front) and was corrected with approximate chart readings. The Rust sort_unstable adoption claim in stars_or_usage was not verified (Rust docs fetch did not show it) and was left unchanged.

tier_reason: First-party blog post with ns/item charts against std::sort. Benchmark code is public (ska_sort_tests_and_benchmarks.cpp), but the post gives no compiler, flags or CPU model, so the tier is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Blog post: 'I wrote a sorting algorithm that's twice as fast as std::sort for many inputs'. On ints from std::geometric_distribution(0.001) it is 'many times faster than std::sort'. For small collections it is 'never slower than std::sort (because it uses std::sort when the collection is too small)', because it stops recursing below 128 elements. Per-type results appear only as ns/item chart images.
corrections.caveats: The repo ships only ska_sort.hpp and ska_sort_tests_and_benchmarks.cpp, with no README and no numbers. The claim lives in the author's 2016 blog post, which states no compiler, flags or CPU model (tier C). The post admits it degrades toward O(n log n) behavior on millions of long strings, and a reader comment reports it slower than std::sort on 1.2 billion uint64_t (unverified). The license (BSL-1.0) is stated only in the file headers; there is no LICENSE file and GitHub reports none. No commits since 2017-05-15.

notes: The quotes match the post. The record's 'once arrays exceed roughly 128 elements' misplaced the 128-element threshold, which is the std::sort fallback cutoff, so claimed_speedup was reworded. The metadata checks out: BSL-1.0 from the file headers, 248 stars, last commit 2017-05-15, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: Code is public (bench/bench.cpp, bench/bars.py). The README states MinGW g++ 6.1.0 -std=c++1z -O2 -march=native, and fallbacks.md says libstdc++ was used, but no CPU model appears in the README, fallbacks.md or the chart axis (bars.py prints only 'Cycles per element'). Tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Approximate, read from the README random-access chart (10^6 ints, cycles per element) (derived from page data). Vergesort beats libstdc++ std::sort on every distribution shown: shuffled ~365 vs ~713 (~2x, via its pdqsort fallback), pipe organ ~22 vs ~885, push front ~15 vs ~858, ascending and descending sawtooth ~63 vs ~325 (~5x). It beats std::stable_sort on most patterns (sawtooth ~63 vs ~165-198) but is slower on 'Alternating' (~307 vs ~185). The author notes the sawtooth patterns are biased toward vergesort.
corrections.workload: Cycles per element (rdtsc, bench/bench.cpp) sorting a std::vector<int> of one million ints under 12 distributions (shuffled, shuffled 16 values, all equal, ascending, descending, pipe organ, push front, push middle, ascending/descending sawtooth, alternating, alternating 16 values). The random-access version is compared against std::sort, std::stable_sort, heapsort and pdqsort. A second chart compares the bidirectional version against std::list::sort, and fallbacks.md compares with/without-vergesort runs over std::sort and std::stable_sort (libstdc++ MinGW 6.1.0), timsort, spreadsort, pdqsort and ska_sort.
corrections.caveats: Numbers appear only as chart images (imgur), so the values are approximate readings. No CPU model is stated anywhere, which caps the tier at C. Built with the old MinGW GCC 6.1.0. The win over std::sort on random data comes from the pdqsort fallback. Slower than std::stable_sort on the 'Alternating' pattern. The bidirectional version is slower than std::list::sort on the sawtooth and alternating patterns.

notes: The record is accurate. claimed_speedup and workload were enriched with approximate chart readings, which show one loss vs std::stable_sort. The metadata checks out: MIT, 73 stars, last commit 2025-11-07 (active), not a fork, not archived. The canonical owner casing is Morwenn/vergesort, default branch trunk.
